stem: During a team huddle, one clinician gives another clinician important information. Which response best demonstrates AHRQ check-back communication?

options.A: Acknowledge the message silently because verbal confirmation is unnecessary when both clinicians are in the same room.
options.B: Repeat the message back and obtain confirmation from the original sender that the information was understood correctly.
options.C: Ask a third team member what the sender probably meant instead of confirming the information with the original sender.
options.D: Write the message down for later review because documentation alone closes the communication loop during the exchange.

rationale: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS defines check-back as a closed-loop communication strategy in which the receiver repeats or confirms the message and the original sender verifies that it was received and understood correctly. Therefore B is correct. A omits feedback, C bypasses the original sender, and D substitutes later documentation for real-time confirmation.
educational_objective: Use check-back communication to close the loop and verify accurate exchange of clinically important information.
source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_version_date: Page last reviewed July 2023; current AHRQ TeamSTEPPS resource as accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: Check-Back definition and examples — receiver directly acknowledges/repeats message and message source confirms accuracy.
source_claim_supported: Check-back is closed-loop communication requiring receiver feedback/repeat-back and sender verification.

source_original.source_detail: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — Check-Back (Repeat-Back): a closed-loop communication strategy in which the sender initiates a message, the receiver accepts and repeats it back, and the sender verifies/corrects the information to confirm shared understanding.
